title: Tire Sizes: Metric P-Metric vs LT vs Flotation — Reading the Sidewall
h1: Tire size decoded — 225/45R17, 33×12.50R15, and load/speed ratings
description: P225/45R17 = 225 mm wide, 45% aspect ratio, 17-inch rim. Overall diameter = rim + 2 × (width × aspect). Plus load index, speed rating, and the ±3% rolling-diameter rule.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against ETRTO Standards Manual 2024, Tire and Rim Association (TRA) Yearbook 2024, JATMA 2024, DOT FMVSS 139, and ISO 4000-1

hero: A sidewall reading '225/45R17 94Y' is not a marketing string — every character is a spec traceable to an international standards manual. 225 mm section width, 45% aspect ratio, radial construction, 17-inch rim, 670 kg load rating per tire, safe to 300 km/h. Get the *outside diameter* wrong when replacing tires and the speedometer, ABS, and ESC all drift out of calibration.
body: The modern tire code is standardised by three regional bodies whose specs converge on the same numbers: **ETRTO** (Europe), **TRA** (North America), **JATMA** (Japan). US federal law (49 CFR 571.139) requires the code on every passenger tire sold.
## Decoding P225/45R17 94Y

> **P** — Passenger (US 'P-metric'). Alternatives: **LT** = Light Truck (higher load), **ST** = Special Trailer, **T** = Temporary spare, no prefix = Euro-metric (identical dimensions to P, ~1% higher load rating).
> **225** — Section width in mm, measured on a specified rim.
> **45** — Aspect ratio = sidewall height ÷ section width × 100. Here 45% × 225 = 101.25 mm sidewall.
> **R** — Radial construction. **B** = bias-belted, **D** = diagonal bias (trailer only).
> **17** — Nominal rim diameter in inches. (Yes, mm/mm/inch on the same tire — historical.)
> **94** — Load index. See table. 94 = 670 kg per tire (2680 kg axle pair, but never load to the exact limit).
> **Y** — Speed rating. See table. Y = 300 km/h (186 mph) sustained.
## Overall diameter — the equation replacements hinge on

> Outside diameter (mm) = (rim × 25.4) + 2 × (section width × aspect / 100)
> 225/45R17: (17 × 25.4) + 2 × (225 × 0.45) = 431.8 + 202.5 = **634.3 mm** (24.97")
> Rolling circumference (loaded, ~97% of geometric): 634.3 × π × 0.97 ≈ 1933 mm/rev
> Revolutions per km ≈ 1,000,000 / 1933 ≈ 517 rev/km

The **±3% rule**: when changing tire size, keep the outside diameter within 3% of factory to stay within the speedometer tolerance mandated by ECE R39 (+10%/−0% error window). Beyond 3%, the ABS/ESC pulse-per-revolution calibration is out of range and the traction control light can trigger persistently.

## Load index (partial table)
Full table: ETRTO Standards Manual, section 2.5. Replacement tire load index must equal or exceed OE — a lower LI is illegal in most jurisdictions.
## Speed rating

| Symbol | km/h | mph | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q | 160 | 100 | Winter tires |
| S | 180 | 112 | Economy summer |
| T | 190 | 118 | Family sedan |
| H | 210 | 130 | Sport sedan |
| V | 240 | 149 | Sport |
| W | 270 | 168 | Ultra-high performance |
| Y | 300 | 186 | Supercar |
| (Y) | >300 | >186 | Bracketed = manufacturer confirmed above Y |

Ratings are for sustained operation on a dyno at 80% of maximum load, ambient 38 °C — not peak spikes. A W-rated tire at 275 km/h for 10 minutes in summer heat is outside its certification even though the tire may survive.
## LT-metric and flotation sizes
Truck tires use LT-metric (**LT265/70R17**) or the older **flotation** format (**33×12.50R15**):

> 33×12.50R15: 33-inch overall diameter × 12.5-inch tread width, 15-inch rim.
> Direct conversion of 33×12.50R15 to metric: 33" = 838 mm OD, tread ≈ 317 mm.
> LT tires carry higher load per size but require higher inflation (typically 50–80 psi vs 32–40 psi P-metric). Never use passenger-car inflation numbers on LT tires.
## Worked example — replacement diameter check
Ford F-150 factory size **275/65R18**:

> OD = 18 × 25.4 + 2 × (275 × 0.65) = 457.2 + 357.5 = 814.7 mm
> Considering 285/70R17 (going up in tire, down in wheel):
> OD = 17 × 25.4 + 2 × (285 × 0.70) = 431.8 + 399 = 830.8 mm
> Delta: (830.8 − 814.7) / 814.7 = +1.98% ✓ (within 3%)
> Speedometer at indicated 60 mph will actually read: 60 × 830.8 / 814.7 = 61.2 mph (true).
## Reading DOT date codes

Every DOT-approved tire has a four-digit date code at the end of the DOT serial: '3324' = week 33 of 2024. Rubber ages; most manufacturers (Michelin, Continental) recommend replacement 6–10 years from manufacture regardless of tread depth, because the plasticizers migrate out and the compound hardens. Check the code on 'new' tires before mounting — dealer inventory older than 3 years is common.
## The five-second recap
Width mm / aspect % R rim inches, load index, speed letter. Replacement OD within ±3% of factory. LI must meet or exceed OE. Date code = week/year of manufacture.

faqs.q: What's the difference between P225 and 225 (no prefix)?
faqs.a: P is US 'P-metric'; no prefix is Euro-metric to ETRTO. Same section width, same overall diameter. Euro-metric tires carry a slightly higher load rating (~1%) at the same LI because the reference inflation pressure differs (2.5 bar vs 35 psi).

faqs.q: My new tires say XL or Reinforced — does that mean I need higher pressure?
faqs.a: Yes. XL (Extra Load) tires reach their rated load only at their higher reference pressure (2.9 bar / 42 psi vs standard 2.5 bar / 36 psi). Match the door-jamb sticker, not the sidewall MAX pressure.

faqs.q: Can I mix speed ratings across axles?
faqs.a: Legally in most jurisdictions the vehicle is limited to the lowest-rated tire fitted. Mixing V-rated fronts with H-rated rears also unbalances high-speed handling — avoid unless installing an OE staggered set.

faqs.q: Does a wider tire hurt fuel economy?
faqs.a: Yes — typically 1–3% per 20 mm of additional section width, from rolling resistance and frontal area. Michelin's internal testing (2019) shows a 245-width tire consuming 2.4% more fuel than a 225 of the same model.

faqs.q: How do I read '95H' vs '95V' — same weight, different letter?
faqs.a: Same load index (95 = 690 kg); different speed rating (H = 210 km/h, V = 240). The compound and construction differ — V has stiffer sidewalls and a stickier tread. Use V-rated when spec'd; do not downgrade.
